newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe 1996/97 budget deficit seen at 10.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe 1996/97 budget deficit seen at 10.3 pct.

text.p: Zimbabwe Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa forecast on Thursday the country's budget deficit for the financial year ended June 30 at 10.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), lower than earlier projections.
But his latest projection is still above a ceiling of 8.5 percent he set last year.
"We had projected it to be about 11.1 percent but the outturn for 1996/97 is now 10.3 percent as a result of revenues which performed well as a result of improved tax collections," he said.

He told Reuters that unbudgeted salary hikes totalling Z$3 billion (U.S.$263 million) which the government awarded to civil servants last year following a series of crippling strikes had widened the spending deficit from the 8.5 percent target.

Murerwa, who presents a new 18-month budget to December 31, 1998, on July 24, could not be drawn into projecting budget targets. The 18-month budget would be a transitional phase from the traditional July to June fiscal year to a calendar year.

Earlier, addressing an annual congress of industrialists in the northern resort town of Victoria Falls, Murerwa said the government would work hard to reduce the budget deficit necessary for a stable macro-economic environment conducive to growth.
"Our country has the human and natural resources to achieve GDP growth rates far in excess of population growth rate of 3.1 percent; the missing link is a conducive macro-economic climate," he said.
Murerwa conceded that the government's budget deficit had, during its first five-year reform programme which ended in 1995, exceeded targets by wide margins.
This led the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund -- which managed Western donor aid for the reforms -- to suspend key balance of payments support to Zimbabwe in 1995.
The two institutions say they are waiting for the new budget on July 24 before deciding on resuming aid for a new tranche of reforms yet to be approved by cabinet.

Murerwa said the government would, under the new reform programme called the Zimbabwe Programme for Economic and Social Transformation, take steps to reduce its expenditure, which accounts for 38 percent of GDP. $1=11.40
